extracted.intended_audience: general readers, TV viewers, and researchers seeking information about the television sitcom Black-ish
extracted.subtask_description: Information and evaluative metrics used to describe and assess the US sitcom Black-ish, including audience ratings, critical aggregator scores, awards, and critical-consensus criteria about the show's themes and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nielsen ratings / viewership metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Season-by-season Nielsen data are reported (timeslot, number of episodes, premiere/end dates, viewers in millions, 18-49 rating/share, TV season rank). Example table headings: 'Timeslot (ET)', '# Ep.', 'Premiered', 'Ended', 'TV Season Rank', 'Viewers (in millions)', '18-49 rating/share'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an empirical measure of audience size and popularity across seasons; numbers are presented per season and used to indicate changes in audience and to contextualize renewals and season rankings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotten Tomatoes approval rating & consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: Rotten Tomatoes approval percentage and average rating are reported per season (e.g., 'Season 1 approval rating of 87% based on 62 reviews, with an average rating of 7.4/10'). Each season entry also includes the site's consensus statement (e.g., 'Although it seems uncertain of its target audience, black-ish ingratiates with a diverse cast and engaging cultural issues.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregator percentage, average score, and the written 'consensus' serve as indicators of critical reception and perceived strengths/weaknesses (target audience clarity, cast, cultural engagement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metacritic weighted average score
rubrics_metrics.description: Metacritic season scores are given as a weighted average out of 100 with the number of critics (e.g., 'Metacritic gave Season 1 a weighted average score of 77 out of 100, based on 34 critics, indicating "generally favorable reviews"').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numeric Metacritic scores plus the associated qualitative label (e.g., 'generally favorable', 'universal acclaim') are used to summarize critical consensus quantitatively and qualitatively across seasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards and nominations
rubrics_metrics.description: Listing of major awards and nominations received by the show and cast (e.g., 'Emmy and Golden Globe nominations for Outstanding Comedy Series', 'TCA Award for Outstanding Achievement in Comedy', Tracee Ellis Ross won 'Golden Globe Award for Best Actress – Television Series Musical or Comedy').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award recognition and nominations function as prestige indicators and are cited to support claims of the show's critical success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of cultural and social issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics repeatedly praised the show for 'addressing important cultural issues' and 'tackling social justice issues' while remaining comedic. Season consensus language includes phrases like 'exploration of race and identity' and 'timely social commentary.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective engagement with cultural/racial/political topics while maintaining entertainment value is presented as a core evaluative criterion for Black-ish's critical success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend of humor and serious topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics note the show's 'ability to blend humor and serious topics while maintaining its relevance' and describe it as 'thought-provoking yet entertaining' or 'sharp and insightful' when successful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining an appropriate tonal balance between comedy and serious cultural commentary is emphasized as central to positive reviews; failure or dip in this balance is noted in mixed reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength of performances (cast)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews single out performances—'the performances of the main cast, particularly Anthony Anderson and Tracee Ellis Ross, were highly praised'—and individual awards (e.g., Ross's Golden Globe) are cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acting quality, especially lead performances, is used as a measurable element in critics' assessments of the series' quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic consistency and freshness
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics commented on season-to-season consistency in comedic energy: phrases such as 'not as consistent as its previous seasons', 'struggles to maintain the same fresh energy', 'slight dip in its comedic edge', and 'mixed or average reviews' appear in season summaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustaining a fresh comedic voice and avoiding repetitiveness across seasons is treated as an evaluative dimension; declines here correlate with more mixed critical reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal/series arc resolution and legacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The final season is evaluated for concluding long-running storylines and emotional payoff (e.g., 'concludes its run with a heartfelt finale that satisfies fans of the series but leaves some lingering questions about its legacy').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How well a series resolves arcs and what legacy it leaves behind is used as a criterion in assessing later-season and series-end evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network content standards / sensitivity to controversial content
rubrics_metrics.description: Production notes indicate that ABC 'shelved' the thirteenth produced episode of season 4 (titled 'Please, Baby, Please') 'due to its controversial content', with the episode later debuting on Hulu.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Networks may withhold or alter episodes for content sensitivity; adherence to or conflict with network content standards can affect episode airing and reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial/creative success signaled by spin-offs and backdoor pilots
rubrics_metrics.description: The article documents that success 'prompted a spin-off titled Grown-ish' and that 'The twenty-third episode of the third season, "Liberal Arts", functioned as a backdoor pilot' for a spin-off; it also documents the ordering and performance of other spin-offs (Mixed-ish, proposed Old-ish).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ability to generate spin-offs and franchise expansion (including successful backdoor pilots and network orders) is treated as an indicator of the show's commercial/creative impact.
